rationale: A wins because it keeps the tension honest: "Duolingo says engagement is at an all-time high. Educators say that's not the same as learning" is the right spine, and it does not pretend time-spent equals learning. B has usable material, but "Duolingo Lets Subscribers Talk to an AI. The Question Is Whether It Can Replace a Human Tutor" wanders past the supplied facts into a market-displacement story it has not earned. A is the set I would hand to a founder without first making them unlearn the overclaims.
gaps_in_A: "Record DAU, profitable, two new product bets in the same quarter" adds "same quarter," which is not in the update. Small, but markets reporters notice invented timing.

"A consumer-tech or company-strategy reporter" is workable, but the chess category angle still needs sharper outlet shape; it is close to general-tech mush unless backed by prior Duolingo non-language context.
The set never explicitly asks for the absolute launch date/source document behind the DAU and beta-session claims; that matters before pitching markets or data reporters.
gaps_in_B: "whether Duolingo is pivoting from language app to AI learning platform" overstates one chess course plus one AI feature into a pivot. That's strategy cosplay until an exec says it.
"whether it can replace a Human Tutor" invents a displacement frame. The update says conversation practice, not tutoring replacement, tutor pricing, or tutor-market impact.
"AI Tutoring Expensive" is sloppy and unsupported. The fact is Max-only video calls; "expensive" and "tutoring" are both doing work the facts did not do.

"The nine-minute AI conversation session is a concrete counterpoint" to shallow-learning criticism confuses engagement with learning. B later admits the proof gap, but the angle headline already sold the weak claim.
